stories.title_en: Secretly Stamping a Mark to Seize Another's Bedding

paragraphs.en: In the countryside there was a man known as You the Shyster, who flouted the law, was a relentless litigant, and preyed on ordinary folk. Word of his shifty ways spread, and everyone feared him and kept their distance. One day he went to the prefectural city by boat and was the first aboard, already seated. The later passengers came crowding in — strangers thrown together by chance, none knowing any of the others — and they sat facing one another in the boat, chatting idly. The talk happened to turn to the touring censor's arrests of litigious troublemakers. Among them was a young man surnamed Qiu, who did not know You the Shyster was on the boat. He said to the group: "I hear that in our county these days You Wu is the worst swindler of all. No one who spends even a short time around him escapes being cheated and hurt. If the touring censor would only get rid of the man, the people could live in peace." You Wu laughed coldly to himself: "What is it to you, that you trumpet my shiftiness and even wish the censor would be rid of me? If I don't swindle this fellow out of something for nothing, my name as a trickster is wasted on me." Noticing that young Qiu's bedding roll was a fine one, he took out a wooden seal, slipped close to a light-colored spot on the felt cover, and secretly stamped a mark on it.

In the evening the boat reached the shore, and each man gathered his luggage and left. You the Shyster trailed behind young Qiu. When they reached the front of the prefectural offices, he snatched the bedding from the servant's carrying pole, saying, "Thanks for the carry—I'll take it from here." Young Qiu lunged to grab it back: "That's my bedding—where do you think you're taking it?" The two of them grappled, neither giving way, until the quarrel carried them right into the magistrate's court. You said, "It's mine—he's trying to force a claim." Qiu said, "He's seizing my property." The magistrate said, "You both claim it. What identifying mark does each of you have?" Qiu said, "I bought it myself and made no mark." You said, "I stamped a seal inside the felt." They opened it up right there in court; You took the wooden seal from his sash and matched it to the mark, and sure enough they were the same. The magistrate said, "This is You's property. How dare Qiu falsely claim it!" He had Qiu given ten strokes of the bamboo, ordered You to take the bedding away, and drove them both out of the yamen. Qiu cursed him: "Who are you, you thief, that you dare cheat me like this? I will pay you back for this!" You Wu said, "That 'You the Shyster' you were talking about on the boat—that's me. What was it to you, going on all day about how shifty I am? So I taught you a lesson: this is how a shyster operates." Only then did Qiu feel regret: "I spoke ill of a man recklessly, and so brought this loss on myself."

Note: Who does not hate a vicious swindler? But if you do not know the man, do not lightly broadcast his faults. He may be listening at your elbow and harbor resentment in his heart. Then, the moment you show a weakness, he will seize the opening and strike you when you least expect it. That is why the ancients thrice sealed their mouths and were careful with their words. Lord Pang's way of leaving peace to his descendants was simply to speak well of everyone. You Wu was wicked, no doubt; yet why did young Qiu gossip about him behind his back, and thereby bring it upon himself that You Wu seized his bedding for nothing? That was the very opposite of Lord Pang's way of securing peace. Thus Confucius detested those who proclaim others' faults, and Mencius warned against speaking of others' failings—both are the sages' way of teaching us to keep resentment at a distance. One cannot be too careful with words.

stories.title_en: A Plaster over the Eyes and an Ingot Snatched

paragraphs.en: In the county town there was a silversmith whose family was fairly well off. The officials responsible for transporting autumn grain-tax silver often entrusted him with melting it down. One day he was melting silver ingots, and feeling there were still spots inside that had not fused through, he boiled and washed them again that night. His shop door had a wide crack in it, and from outside one could see in. A crook bought a large medicinal plaster and crept up at night to peek. He watched the man finish washing two ingots and set them by the furnace. Then the crook, outside, began to groan in pain and cried: "Open the door!" The silversmith asked: "Who is it?" The crook answered from outside: "I've been badly beaten by a thieving brute. I beg you, let me warm a plaster at your furnace so I can put it on." The silversmith opened the door and let him in. The crook limped along, hands trembling, groaning in pain, his hair a tangled mess, head bowed. He warmed the large plaster at the furnace until it softened, then slapped it with both hands straight onto the silversmith's face, snatched one ingot, and ran. The burning pain was more than the silversmith could stand; he tore the plaster off in a frenzy, but the ingot was already gone with the thief. He shouted "Thief!" and rushed out in pursuit, but had no idea which way the man had gone. After chasing a few dozen paces in vain, he could only go back, bitter and heartsick.

Note: This crook's act — groaning in pain, begging to be let in, scorching his skin with a hot plaster by the furnace — was truly hard to see through. But an ingot is a weighty thing; had he put it away first and only then opened the door, there would have been no loss. Let those who come after take note: anyone carrying silver must never lightly let a suspicious stranger get close.

stories.title_en: Throwing Lime in the Eyes to Snatch the Silver

paragraphs.en: Sun Tao was a man from Henan. He regularly bought cotton cloth and sold it in Jianning Prefecture, Fujian. One night, he was melting silver at the shop of Wang Liu, a silversmith. After the melting was finished, two packets of silver were placed on the table facing one another. While the two men were still comparing the silver, a thief walked straight into the shop and flung lime into their eyes. With their hands full trying to save their sight, they couldn't stop the thief from taking the packets of silver off the table and making off with them. Tao chased after him for dear life. Just as he was about to catch up, the thief dropped one packet on the ground. Tao picked it up and returned; when he opened it at the silversmith's shop, it turned out to be all iron. In the end, there was no trail left to catch him.

Note: As the saying goes, “A thief is a petty man, but his wits outrun a gentleman's.” How true that is! When he first entered the shop, he flung lime to burn their eyes, leaving them no time to look after their money; when the chase was nearly upon him, he dropped a packet on the ground to block the pursuit and make off with it. Was this merely the thief perfecting his biding of time, and careless keeping inviting theft? Yet Tao’s own habitual carelessness had brought it about. Be warned by this, for just as a man who has been choked becomes careful with his food—that is the lesson to take away.

stories.title_en: Robbed by Crooks in Broad Daylight While Relieving Himself

paragraphs.en: Wang Heng was from Yangzhou Prefecture in the Nanjing region, serving as a clerk in the prefectural office. Having completed his two terms, he was due to go up to the capital to attend to official business. Poor and with no funds of his own, he borrowed over ten taels of silver from relatives and friends and set out alone for Beijing to cover the costs of his appointment. Upon arriving in the capital, he relieved himself on the grass near the drill ground. No sooner had he pulled down his trousers than two crooks seized him, cursing him as they cleaned out his clothes: "You thief—you stole our clothes!" They immediately snatched his clothes along with his silver and fled. By the time he got up, fastened his trousers, and gave chase, the two crooks were already far away. Heng had been traveling for many days and was exhausted; though he chased them for dear life, he could not catch them. Choked with regret and rage, he had no choice but to beg for travel money at the Huitong government hostel and head home to make other arrangements later.

Note: A lone traveler away from home must guard against robbery not only in out-of-the-way places. Even when relieving himself on a main road, he should take off his trousers and keep them tucked under his arm. Then, if some rogue means mischief, he can get up and run, or stand and fight. Wang Heng knew no such caution, and the crooks took his clothes and his silver, every last bit of them. At that point, with no travel money to be found, what became of his prospects? Had his fellow clerks at the Huitong Hostel not lent him the money for the journey back, he would have ended up little better than a beggar.
